...sent down from on high a Cabalistic spirit <note>original: "Cabalisticum animum"; referring to a divinely inspired mindset for interpreting mystical traditions</note>, destined to illuminate holy religion among all nations. But since, until this time, the Cabalistic sun had not yet risen openly for the Latin or Greek peoples, that famous Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a brilliant Renaissance philosopher who sought to harmonize all knowledge and introduced Jewish mysticism to the Christian West.</note>—the glory of Italy and a man of remarkable piety—strove to spread the Cabalistic light from the Hebrews to the Latins, believing it to be extremely beneficial to religion. To this end, he formulated many Cabalistic conclusions <term>conclusiones: the 900 theses Pico proposed to defend in public debate in Rome in 1486</term> according to his own thinking. 

(These I have very recently explained and published for common use). Furthermore, he inserted many sayings worthy of note from the more secret Theologians <note>likely referring to the authors of the Zohar or other Kabbalistic texts</note> into his nine hundred conclusions, which he left untouched <note>original: "intacta reliquit"; meaning Pico presented the ideas but did not provide the full commentary or explanation for them.</note>. 

As for me, although I have been a devotee of the name of Cabala <term>Cabala: from the Hebrew 'Qabbalah,' meaning 'received tradition'; a form of Jewish mysticism that Renaissance scholars adapted to support Christian doctrines</term> for many years, I have undertaken such a weighty task not under my own auspices, but under yours. In commenting on these matters, I hope that divine help will not be lacking for so necessary and so pious a duty. 

But for those who bring forth new things, the rage of a thousand Scyllas and a thousand Charybdises <note>classical monsters from the Odyssey, representing the overwhelming and dangerous opposition faced by innovators</note> immediately barks against them. There is no shortage of rivals—or rather, malevolent men—who tear at them with their mouths, pour poison upon them, and spread a blasphemous opinion of them throughout the entire world. Truly, these critics should have considered how much opportunity for mockery they provide to heretics and Jews; for when those groups see the very men they thought were the assertors and defenders of Christian dogma now being refuted and struck down, they rejoice that these defenders are being attacked by their own people, whom...

<meta>This page continues the dedication by Brother Archangelo to Bernardino Aiano. Having previously discussed Pico della Mirandola’s efforts to bring the "Cabalistic light" to the Latin world, Archangelo now argues for the practical utility of this mystical science in defending the faith and appeals to Bernardino for patronage.</meta>

...they could not conquer in a hostile manner. What teaching is found to be more fit for overcoming Jewish disbelief <note>original: "iudaicam perfidiam"; literally 'Jewish perfidy,' a common polemical term in the Renaissance referring to the Jewish rejection of Christian claims</note> and for silencing the mouths of heretics than the science which is called Cabala <term>Cabala: a Renaissance Christian adaptation of Jewish Kabbalah, used to find hidden proofs for Christian doctrines within Hebrew tradition</term>? 

Oh, what a crime—which no one has ever sufficiently shuddered at, as is only right—I weep that such great glory of the more secret theologians <note>referring to the mystical authors of the Kabbalistic tradition</note> is withering away like little flowers! For they, long ago moved by mercy, prepared noble garden springs and deep wells of living waters with an untiring spirit for the sheep of Christ the Messiah. 

But to which protector I should devote these works, or whose concern they should be, I do not know, unless you, most illustrious Bernardino <note>Bernardino Aiano, the patron to whom this work is dedicated</note>, show yourself merciful and pious toward them. In this way, the more secret theologians will be able to boast of enjoying the air of Parma <note>original: "aura Parmensi"; implying that Bernardino’s protection provides a safe and favorable environment in his home city of Parma</note>. Therefore, receive most kindly these sayings of the most skilled Cabalists <term>Cabalistarum: scholars or practitioners of the Kabbalah</term>, restored to light by this modest explanation of ours and dedicated to you. Consult with them often; let them be your most faithful companions and support you. 

Like Job, they have been made rich from poverty; and like Mordecai <note>a biblical figure from the Book of Esther who rose from humble status to high honor</note>, they have become distinguished from a humble state. Like the servant of Abraham <note>referring to Eliezer, who brought precious jewels to Rebecca as part of a marriage proposal on behalf of Isaac</note>, they carry in their bags an innumerable wealth of jewels, with which your soul—as a Rebecca—may be adorned and honored. Therefore, I pray that you may be to these sacred, more secret theologians what Zacchaeus <note>the tax collector in the Gospel of Luke who climbed a tree to see Jesus and welcomed him into his home</note> was to Christ, so that through their words, salvation may come to your house in Christ Jesus.

# ARCHANGELO
## OF THE ORDER OF FRIARS MINOR
# FROM BORGONOVO IN THE TERRITORY OF
## PIACENZA, ON THE EXPOSITIONS
->of the sayings of the most distinguished secret theologians,<-
->that is, the Cabalists.<-

### *An Apologetic Preface to the Reader.*

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'I' featuring a figure in a landscape holding a long cross or staff, enclosed within a rectangular frame with ornate botanical scrolls.</image-desc>

AMONG so many varied and manifold gifts which we have received from God—the best and greatest giver of all good things—dearest reader, no one who thinks rightly will believe that anything nobler or more health-giving has fallen to mortals than wisdom. For this governs the whole life of man. It teaches, first and foremost, how the soul is to be formed toward God, and then how one’s entire life is to be established. Indeed, there is a knowledge of both divine and human things. The former, which is concerned with divine matters, is received in the heart alone through informed faith <term>informed faith: in Latin, "fides formata," a theological concept referring to faith that is not merely intellectual but is "formed" or animated by love and charity</term>. The latter, however, which regards human internal and external actions, is passed down to posterity on parchment. This second type arranges the exterior and civil life of man and draws the soul toward the consideration of created things. But that first kind is a certain most vigorous spirit, which cannot be expressed by the "killing letter" <note>original: "occidente litera"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life." Archangelo is contrasting literal, written laws with the living spiritual truth of the Cabala</note>, but is written by the finger of God in the hearts of the faithful, according to that testimony of Jeremiah: *I the Lord will put my law in their inward parts, and write it upon their hearts.* <note>Jeremiah 31:33</note>

<summary>In this opening of his preface, Archangelo of Borgonovo defines wisdom as the greatest divine gift, distinguishing between external human knowledge recorded in books and the internal, spiritual wisdom written by God directly on the heart.</summary>

<keywords>Archangelo of Borgonovo, wisdom, Cabala, informed faith, Jeremiah, spiritual law, Christian Kabbalah, theology</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded with a distinction between human knowledge recorded on parchment and divine knowledge held in the heart. It ended by referencing the "killing letter" (2 Corinthians 3:6). This page continues the sentence and the argument, using the catchword "enim" to bridge into the necessity of rediscovering ancient mystical texts.</meta>

and I will be their **God**, and they shall be my people <note>original: "ero eorum Deus, ipsiq; erunt populus meus"; a biblical promise found in Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 37:27, signaling a direct, internal relationship with the Divine</note>. For the grasping of this wisdom, among other things that are sought after, I observe nothing more desirable, nothing more useful, and nothing more holy than the fact that the monuments of the most ancient orthodox and secret theologians <term>secret theologians: a reference to "theologi secretiores," or practitioners of mystical theology, specifically Cabalists</term> are now emerging into the light everywhere. For what could have ever been more necessary for the welfare of the Church, or for the convenience and progress of studies? Since the Church will stand safer and firmer through works of this kind—even through these very small safeguards—and the intellects of these men are always trained toward a better harvest.

For antiquity itself possesses a certain peculiar gift in handling difficult matters and investigating divine affairs, which even **Marcus Cicero** seems to have understood when, discussing weighty causes in his inquiries, he says: "Men who lived in those ancient ages, the closer they were to the world's birth, the more blessed they were in intellect and mind" <note>original: "Homines qui priscis illis seculis extiterunt, quo propiores nascenti mundo erant, eo ingenio ac mente fuisse beatiores"; a paraphrase of Cicero's argument in *Tusculan Disputations* that the ancients had a clearer view of truth by proximity to the source of creation</note>. If he seems to have spoken aptly regarding pagan men, how much more rightly can we affirm it of our own? And even more so of the secret theologians, who, in the explanation of the sacred scriptures, do not delay the reader with various and subtle questions, nor do they pursue battles of useless words and superfluous conflicts (from which envy, contention, and slander usually sprout).

But they are entirely engaged in this: to diligently extract the spirit hiding within the letter of the law <term>letter of the law: the literal or "surface" meaning of the text</term> as if from a kind of shell <note>original: "corticem"; literally "bark" or "rind." This is a common metaphor in mystical thought for the outer layer of scripture that protects but also hides the inner spiritual truth</note>, so that they might thus affect the mind, change the perception, lift the soul upward, and finally transform the whole man, as great as he is. And in performing this, they do not anxiously gather outside aids, but rather, following the Apostle's opinion, they "compare spiritual things with spiritual" <note>original: "spiritualibus spiritualia conferunt"; a direct reference to 1 Corinthians 2:13, the method of interpreting scripture through scripture</note>, and they blend together a vast power of the scriptures, preserved from all sides out of the sacred writings as if from fountains (not without great judgment). Which...

He cites Cicero to support the idea that more ancient thinkers were closer to divine truth.</summary>
<keywords>Cabalists, Marcus Cicero, spiritual vs literal, mystical theology, scriptural interpretation, soul transformation</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>The previous page discussed the superiority of ancient, secret theological wisdom. It concluded with a reference to Cicero’s belief that the ancients were closer to the world's divine origin and thus had a clearer intellect. This page begins by applying this logic to the study of the Bible, specifically why Christian scholars must consult Hebrew sources to understand the literal foundation of the scriptures.</meta>

For as it pertains to the literal sense of the letter, it must be sought primarily from the Hebrews, since they, being devoted to this task, have observed it with painstaking care. Because of this, [Nicholas of] Lyra <term>Nicholas of Lyra: a 14th-century Franciscan scholar whose commentaries became the standard for literal biblical interpretation</term> almost always followed **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: "Rabbi Salomonem"; refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous Jewish commentator, whose literal explanations of the Hebrew Bible were essential to Christian Hebraists</note>. For just as eyes accustomed to the clearest light see less accurately in dark places (as **Plato** says) because their vision is hindered, so the eyes of our theologians, having dwelt in the spiritual light of the mystical sense, will sometimes perceive less clearly those shadowy difficulties than those who are accustomed to the darkness <note>The author suggests that Jewish scholars are "accustomed to the darkness" of the literal/law-bound text, whereas Christian theologians are dazzled by "mystical light." This reflects the typical period view that the Old Testament literal meaning was a "shadow" of the New.</note>.

For although we have obtained this knowledge from the Hebrews so that we might prove the mysteries of our faith through them and oppose them when they disagree with us, we shall nevertheless note many things worthy of knowledge in our own works—as if taking them from unjust possessors—and bestow them upon the true Israelites <note>true Israelites: a term the author uses here to refer to Christians, who believed they were the spiritual heirs to the biblical promises</note>, so that they may not boast of having any good thing that the Church does not also possess. **[Pico della] Mirandola** believes **Jerome** would have done all these things in his introduction to the Psalms, had he not been so occupied in the work of translation that he had no leisure to interpret the Law of **Moses**. Others have not touched upon Hebrew literature at all.

The allegorical sense (as we have written elsewhere) relates to the literal sense just as matter relates to form <term>matter and form: an Aristotelian concept where "matter" is the raw stuff and "form" is the invisible quality or essence that gives it meaning and identity</term>. It is, in a way, a species of meaning that belongs properly and uniquely to the sacred letters, such that the things being discussed also signify something else themselves. And just as the form is not seen by us, but rather the matter clothed in "accidents" <term>accidents: in philosophy, the physical characteristics of a thing (color, shape) that are not part of its essential nature</term> through which we are permitted to contemplate the forms, in no different way are we carried forward to the allegorical sense—which we cannot perceive with eyes of flesh—by the help of the literal sense. 

Therefore, allegory is established as the goal of understanding. For this reason, it is not appropriate to seek it in everything, for not all things are the "end" or goal of everything; rather, many things have arisen and been established both for the sake of the goal and out of necessity. The beginning of this true and heavenly wisdom is defined as the fear of the Lord <note>original: "timor Domini"; a reference to Psalm 111:10 and Proverbs 1:7</note>. For this gift of **God** is not sent down into a malevolent soul, nor is that heavenly treasure [poured] into an earthen ves— <note>original: "vasi fictili Thesaurus ille cœ-"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7, where the "treasure" of the gospel is held in "earthen vessels." The text cuts off here at the start of the word "heavenly" (coelestis).</note>

<summary>The author argues that Hebrew scholarship is essential for the literal understanding of the Bible, serving as the necessary foundation for higher allegorical and mystical interpretations. He uses Aristotelian concepts to explain how the literal text acts as the "matter" that carries the spiritual "form" of the scripture.</summary>

<keywords>Nicholas of Lyra, Rashi, Pico della Mirandola, St. Jerome, literal sense, allegorical sense, matter and form, Christian Hebraism, Plato, Fear of the Lord</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument for the study of ancient Hebrew wisdom, transitioning from the literal interpretation of scripture to the mystical insights of the Kabbalists and the institutional requirements for linguistic study in the Church.</meta>

[Heavenly things] are committed, or cast before swine: to the children of God alone, and the citizens of the celestial kingdom, who can cry from the heart “Abba, Father” <note>original: "Abba pater"; an Aramaic and Latin invocation of God the Father from the New Testament (Romans 8:15)</note>, is this spirit delivered—to one in this way, to another in that. Only Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt, received this spirit without measure. The philosophers lacked this wisdom, as did all who were alienated from God. Therefore, they vanished into their own thoughts, and their hearts were darkened as they groped like the blind along a wall; like those without eyes, they felt their way, stumbling at noon as if in the darkness—to use the words of **Isaiah** <note>Reference to Isaiah 59:10</note>. These were content with only worldly prudence and secular wisdom. Although such wisdom is great and especially necessary for this domestic and peaceful life, it offers no support for attaining the future life unless celestial wisdom is added.

For “knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” <note>original: "Scientia enim inflat, charitas autem aedificat"; a quote from 1 Corinthians 8:1</note>. But if knowledge is supported by charity, then earthly wisdom migrates into the heavenly, and darkness is turned into light. Therefore, excellent Reader, receive from the number of those whom antiquity commends the sayings of the foremost **Kabbalists** <term>Cabalistarum: practitioners of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that Christian scholars in the Renaissance believed contained hidden truths about Christ</term>. These are like divine utterances, illuminating a keen intellect and giving off the "good odor of Christ."

Yet I do not wish to boast too arrogantly here of either my own work or the genius of the authors; indeed, if you look within a little more diligently, I believe you will not find fault with our industry, and you will greatly admire the dignity of the authors. All these things must be weighed so that we do not err, and also so that we do not give the enemies of the Church an opportunity to mock us as if we were ignorant. Therefore, it was most wisely decreed in the **Council of Vienne** <term>Concilio Vienensi: a Catholic Church council held in 1311–1312</term> (as noted by Pope Clement in the decree regarding teachers <note>original: "Clementina vnica de Magistris"; refers to the *Clementines*, a collection of canon law</note>) that in the major universities—those of **Bologna**, **Paris**, **Salamanca**, and **Oxford** <note>original: "Bononiensi, Parisiensi, Salamantino, atque Exoniensi"; while "Exoniensi" literally refers to Exeter, in the context of this specific decree from the Council of Vienne, Oxford is the university intended</note>—and especially wherever the Roman Curia happens to reside, schools should be established for the study of

<summary>This page argues that secular philosophy is insufficient for salvation without divine wisdom and introduces the "Kabbalists" as a source of mystical truth. <meta>This page follows a discussion on the limitations of worldly wisdom and the necessity of divine illumination, moving now into the practical requirement for studying biblical languages—Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, and Arabic—to uncover hidden scriptural truths.</meta>

of different <term>languages</term> <note>original: "Idiomatum"; here referring to the primary languages of biblical scholarship</note>: namely, Hebrew, Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldei"; often used in this period to refer to Aramaic</note>, Greek, and Arabic. And he himself assigns the reasons, saying: so that the learned may know, evidently, how to translate faithfully into Latin and to teach others, and so that men of different languages might be more easily and better instructed. For the meanings of Holy Scripture are more clearly gathered and more easily persuaded to others in one's own mother tongue (as they say) than in a foreign one. Nor has God, the Best and Greatest, roused in vain so many and such great men in this time of ours who are students of Hebrew. This, I believe, He does so that those mysteries which have until now lain hidden may be brought forth into the light. Therefore, we ought not to despise such things, unless perhaps we wish to appear ignorant, thereby offering an occasion for scorn to those who wish to gather the true meanings of scripture.

Now, however, most honest reader, it is time that we defend the truth itself, rather than the sayings of men. For your goodness knows very well that in many matters **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> differs from **Augustine**, and **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher</note> from **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274)</note> and **Henry** <note>Likely Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293)</note>. Hence, the divine oracles <note>original: "oracula"; referring to the biblical texts as direct utterances from God</note> themselves must be diligently inspected and considered with a proper examination, from which (as **Plato** rightly perceived) we ought to be taught concerning divine matters. It is also to be noted that in interpreting the scriptures, we should be bound to no one, nor "swear by the words of any master" <note>original: "iurare in verba alicuius Magistri"; a classical idiom from Horace, meaning to follow a teacher blindly</note> except the most holy Church and the Holy Scripture, whose passages (as is the custom of truly wise men) we ought to explain one by another. We should not, however, explain them through philosophy, or through the sayings of those who are devoted to philosophy; for **Paul** says: "See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the tradition of men" <note>original: "Videte ne quis vos seducat per philosophiam..."; a quote from Colossians 2:8</note>. In these and in all my sayings and writings, I always submit myself to the judgment of the most holy Roman Church and of expert men, and I believe nothing more or less than what she, my mother the Church, believes. Farewell, and pray to God for me.

### DOCTRINES.

[By the] virtue <note>original: *virtute*. The first syllable is on the previous page.</note> of the Divine Name, it is granted; and the priest, wishing to perform sacred rites for God, entered into the sanctuary, or into the Holy of Holies. And this he did when he wished to procure atonement for the people on the Day of Forgiveness, which the Hebrews call *Yom Kippur* <note>original: **יום כפורים** (*iom hachepurim*)</note>. This day was ordained in the seventh month—a number certainly associated with release <note>The number seven in biblical numerology often signifies completion, rest (the Sabbath), or the release of debts (the Sabbatical year).</note>—and on the tenth day of the moon of that same month, at which time a fast and the "affliction of the soul" were commanded, so that the people might more easily obtain forgiveness. And the animals that were required to be offered had to be clean, whole, and without blemish, unless they were offered voluntarily, as is held in *Leviticus*. And this is because stainless things are owed to a stainless God; moreover, it is especially commanded that they not lack an ear or a tail. For whatever animal we offer signifies that our own **animal nature** <term>animal nostrum: the lower, sensory, or "bestial" soul of a human being, which must be disciplined and offered to God</term> is to be offered to God as a **stainless sacrifice**, pleasing to God, just as *Paul* teaches the *Romans*. We must watchfully provide for this animal nature of ours so that ears are not lacking. For through no other sense can a human, while he is in an animal body, grasp Divine things except through hearing. Because **faith**, in which we are taught about divine matters, **comes from hearing**, as *Paul* says. Such animals must also have a tail, which signifies **perseverance** in good works. ...[divine matters, it is required] for two lambs to be brought: one for the evening, the other for the morning. The **evening sacrifice** <note>original: *sacrificium uespertinum*</note> was performed to appease the accusers appearing before the **tribunal of justice** <note>In Cabalistic thought, this refers to the *Sefirah* of *Gevurah* (Judgment), often associated with the "North."</note>, who accused the uncircumcised as if they were guilty of **original sin** <note>original: *culpa originali*</note> not yet expiated. But the **morning sacrifice** was performed to obtain the grace of mercy and piety from the tribunal located in the south <note>The "South" is traditionally associated with the *Sefirah* of *Chesed* (Mercy).</note>, and God required these two lambs to be offered forever. 

Many other sacrifices were also performed. For sacrifices possess a certain **symbolism** <term>symbolum: a mystical correspondence or connection between the physical act and the spiritual reality</term> with the one to whom they are offered, and with those who are being purified. This symbolism is so hidden, however, that the human intellect cannot grasp it, although everyone acknowledges that sacrifices are necessary. For sacrifice is a kind of natural intermediary between God and man. 

For to sacrifice to God—as **Aristotle** says in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, and **Proclus** in his book *On Prayers and Petitions*, and likewise **Plato**, **Plotinus**, and **Porphyry**—is **proper to man** <note>original: *homini proprium*</note>, just as lowing is to oxen and barking to dogs. And they further add that whoever scorns to perform this deserves to be cast out from human nature and to have the name of "human" denied to them. For sacrifice is "proper" to man in the **fourth way** <note>In the logic of the time, a "fourth mode property" is a characteristic that belongs to every member of a species, to that species alone, and at all times (like "the ability to laugh" for humans).</note>; for it belongs to every man, to man alone, and always to him. Moreover, the offering of this or that sacrifice for this or that atonement, although most fitting in the natural order...

->### DOCTRINES<-

[made this way], yet they were instituted by God: since human inquiry is not sufficient to discover those things which God specifically requires for our **atonement** <term>expiatio: the act of making amends or purification for sin</term> according to the order of heavenly things, alongside the things to be purified and the purifying sacrifices, so that the heavenly powers may be rendered appeased and may refrain from the execution of the punishment which the committed sins deserve. 

For the blood of animals seems to purge the sin contracted in the flesh from the blood of our animal nature, according to that saying of the Apostle: *almost everything is purified with blood* <note>original: *omnia penè mundantur in sanguine*; a reference to Hebrews 9:22</note>. He says "almost," because vessels of earth and bronze shall be purified with water; nor indeed was it without reason that man—who is the bond of all things, contains all things, and holds the greatest **symbolism** <term>symbolum: a mystical correspondence between the physical and spiritual worlds</term> in his lower part, in which and through which the beginning of sin is contracted—was purified along with the animals through the blood of spotless animals, which were offered by the priest of the Law. 

However, certain other sacrifices existed earlier; such as the fruits of the earth and the firstfruits, as is evident from the case of **Abel** <note>Abel offered the firstlings of his flock, while Cain offered the fruits of the ground; here the author discusses the evolution of these offerings.</note> and from the observance of the **law of nature** <term>lex naturae: the moral law inherent in human nature, prior to the written Ten Commandments</term>. And through these, for the atonement of sins, God was rendered satisfied, as Paul testifies: *They are a law unto themselves, who show the work of the law written in their hearts* <note>original: *Ipsi sunt sibi lex, qui legis opus in suis cordibus scriptum ostendunt*; Romans 2:14-15</note>, and so forth. And just as the Written Law was more perfect than the law of nature, so God clearly instituted in it more perfect sacrifices of animals; for animals [are more excellent than] fruits...

Thus, once Wisdom is produced—since she is most like the one who produced her and emanates from him by a natural progression—she receives the name of "Son." <note>In Latin theology, *Sapientia* (Wisdom) is feminine, but it is used here to describe the second person of the Trinity, the Son (Jesus), following the tradition of "Christ the Wisdom of God."</note> 

Indeed, the **Love** sprouting from both is called the **Spirit**, and the bond between them both. To this Love, which connects the parent with the offspring, correspond the **Seraphic** and **Cherubic** orders. For the one full of wisdom and beauty <note>The Cherubim, whose name was traditionally interpreted as "fullness of knowledge."</note> corresponds to the Son, who is the highest Wisdom, called the Father's "delight" and the splendor and beauty of all things. 

The **Thrones**, however, serve the Father; sitting upon them, He glories in the continual production of the Word and the Spirit, and through them they judge the world, as the **Psalm** testifies: *He has prepared His throne for judgment.* <note>original: *Parauit in iudicio thronum suum*; referencing Psalm 9:7.</note> This seat the Father grants to the Son, bestowing upon him every kind of power to judge: as he himself testifies in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> saying: I...

# ->DOCTRINES<- <note>original: *DOGMATA*</note>

God—as **Elohim Zabaoth** <note>original: אלהים צבאות; "God of Hosts"</note>—creates living beings <note>original: *animalia*; here referring to the eighth rank of the celestial hierarchy, often associated with the "Sons of God" or *Beni Elohim*.</note>. In the ninth place are the **Cherubim** <note>original: כרובים</note>, through whom God—as **Shaddai** <note>original: *sadai*; the Almighty</note>—cares for the human race. Beneath these is the spiritual <note>original: *animasticus*; relating to the soul or the breath of life.</note> order called the **Issim** <note>original: אִישִׁים; "Men" or "Souls"</note>, who are heroes, strong and blessed men; through them, God—as **Adonai** <note>original: אדני; "My Lord"</note>—bestows the gift of prophecy.

Our theologians <note>referring to Christian scholars of the period.</note>, however, establish a threefold distinction of angels, dividing each of these into three further orders. This results in three distinctions comprising nine orders in total, which they call hierarchies or "choirs."

In the **higher hierarchy**, they place the **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones**. These are super-celestial spirits who contemplate the order of Divine Providence: the first focus on the goodness of God, the second on His essence, and the third on His wisdom.

In the **middle hierarchy**, they place the **Dominions**, **Virtues**, and **Powers**. These are worldly spirits <note>original: *mundanos spiritus*; spirits tasked with the governance of the created universe.</note> who work together to govern the world. Of these, the first issue the commands that the others carry out; the second administer the heavens and sometimes strive to perform miracles; the third ward off those things that seem able to disturb the divine law.

In the **lower hierarchy**, they place the **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**. These descend to care for the lower realms. Of these, the first group cares for public affairs, specifically overseeing princes, magistrates, provinces, and individual kingdoms.

But they are called "many" in relation to us, upon whom many benefits and diverse gifts trickle down through diverse <term>channels</term> <note>original: *canales*; in Kabbalistic thought, these are the pathways (or *Sefirot*) through which divine energy flows into the physical world.</note>. For example, this name **אל** (*El*), which we have interpreted as "God," fosters all things and assists everyone with the highest piety and mercy, for that is what is proper to him; and for this reason, grace is attributed to him. To the name **אלהים** (*Elohim*), [judgment is attributed], because through it come severe punishments, slaughters, and men of war. Hence, God exercising his power by punishing the wicked is called a "man of war," of whom Jeremiah says:

> The Lord is with me like a mighty warrior, 
> or like a powerful crusher. 

Therefore he attributes judgment to himself; and the angels serving him are rightly called *Elohim*, that is, "sons of *Elohim*." *Elohim* therefore signifies terror and dread. Hence, the northern place is assigned to him: from

**He is a true sphere**, and in every progression He proceeds in a spherical order; bringing all things back into Himself, just as they first proceeded from Him. Hence, this mass of created things cannot tend toward anything else except toward Him, whose image it bears.

Furthermore, all the lines of a circle going out from the center to the circumference, and from the circumference back to the center, signify that all creatures emanating from the center of the highest sphere tend toward the circumference of that same sphere as if toward their ultimate goal. Just as all <term>accidents</term> <note>original: *accidentia*; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are qualities (like color or shape) that cannot exist on their own and must belong to a "substance."</note> rest upon <term>substance</term>, <note>original: *substantiæ*; the underlying reality or "thing" that supports qualities.</note> which is their subject and support; so too all created things—which are like accidents in respect to the **First Cause**, who exists by His own power—rest upon Him on whom they depend. They are contained in Him as if in a support. In Him they wander as if they were being unfolded into their own proper forms, and they look toward Him and tend toward Him as if toward their own rightful place and home. 

Therefore, without Him, they cannot long persist, being like foreigners in a strange land; instead, they busily strive to return to Him. This is especially true for **man**, who contains all things by his virtue and power, as **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the *Hermetica*, a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts.</note> teaches. -># OF THE KABBALISTS<-

It is required that the one who prays be united with the one invoked, who is indeed the head of the divine names, tending toward mercy as much as toward justice. By appearing in the fire, however, God wished to teach and indicate that He is Himself a fire, and possesses a fiery name and a fiery power. One must work with this name: the Tetragrammaton is good for the good, as is clear in the case of Moses. God had filled him with such divinity that he was full of God, and was even called "the God of Pharaoh" <note>A reference to Exodus 7:1, where God tells Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh."</note>; for he had to exercise the power of divinity against Pharaoh himself. 

Hence, Moses was a true king, anointed with divinity. Therefore, just as it is a name of mercy, so it is also a name of justice, as is clear from what has been said above.

**The Kabbalistic Doctor:** Adam’s sin was the cutting off of the Kingdom from the other plants. <note>original: "truncatio regni à cæteris plantis"; in Kabbalistic thought, this refers to "cutting the shoots," a metaphor for isolating the final divine emanation, *Malkuth* (Kingdom), from its source, thereby disrupting the balance of the divine realm.</note>

**Friar Archangelus:** <note>Likely Archangelus of Borgonovo, a Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist who wrote influential commentaries on the "Kabbalistic Dogmas" of Pico della Mirandola.</note> The Kabbalists’ method of teaching is through parables, figures, and similitudes. For a parable signifies, according to its meaning, a comparison of dissimilar things; for this reason, parabolic speech is good. First, because it is given through sensible things—things we can perceive with our senses—from which the ignorant as well as the learned are able to grasp the meaning. This is clear from that famous parable: *A sower went out to sow his seed* <note>original: "Exijt, qui seminat seminare semen suũ"; a reference to the Parable of the Sower found in the Gospels (e.g., Luke 8:5).</note>; for everyone understands what a seed is, and what a field is, and so on. Second, because the stories told are impressed upon the mind: for a parable serves as a substitute for an artificial memory. Third, because our knowledge has its origin in the senses: therefore, it shares a common bond with sensible parables. Fourth, because there is great spiritual consolation in the way a parable agrees with the spiritual reality figured by it. For Paul, in agreement with this teaching, says: *The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.* <note>original: "inuisibilia Dei à creatura mundi per ea, quæ facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur"; a quote from Romans 1:20, suggesting that the physical world reflects divine truths.</note> Here, therefore, this doctor, treating the sin of Adam parabolically and learnedly, does not follow the method of our usual theologians. Thus, the sin of our first parents consists in the fact that they did not obey the Divine command, which was that they should not eat of the fruit, or rather that wood; which wood is the Law. <meta>This page continues the theological analysis of Adam's fall, moving from the divine remedy (the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world) to a systematic categorization of the nature of sin according to Church Fathers and Kabbalistic thinkers. -># DOCTRINES <-

...ciently and finally. For the foundation of his sin was disobedience. For sin, as **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> testifies, is a word, a deed, or a desire against the law of God. Or, it is a transgression of the law and disobedience to heavenly commands, according to **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan.</note>. The root of this was **greed** <note>original: "auaritia"; in this context, it refers to a disordered desire for more than what God had granted.</note>, which arose in the salty earth of disobedience. The beginning of this was **pride**; which sprouted from the root of greed. Its end was **gluttony** <note>original: "gula"; specifically the consumption of the forbidden fruit.</note>. Therefore, the sin of Adam was an impulse of disobedience, rooted in greed, initiated by pride, and finally completed in gluttony.

Just as it lingered with those above, so it did with those below. ...Sephiroth <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "Sephiroth" from the previous page</note>. In Adam’s transgression, God commanded **Malchuth** <term>Malchuth: "Kingdom," the tenth and lowest Sephirah, representing the physical world and the presence of the Divine on Earth</term>—the lowest of all the **Sephiroth** <term>Sephiroth: the ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite God reveals Himself and interacts with the universe</term>—acting as the dispenser of holy anointings <note>original: "sanctorum chrismatum"</note>, that she should not pour a good influence into Adam. This is the manner of God according to the Kabbalists: when He ensures that the [lack of] merit of the unjust is answered, He commands His "Kingdom"—that is, the dispenser **Malchuth**—not to pour goodness into that person, as if she stood cut off from the other "plants" <note>referring to the other branches or emanations of the Divine Tree</note>. This is what is called **to prune the last plant** <note>original: "truncare ultimam plantam"; a technical Kabbalistic term for a spiritual defect where the lowest Sephirah is perceived as severed from the divine flow above</note>.

The sentence of this act fell not only upon Adam, but also upon all his descendants, whom it infected—indeed, it infected the whole world. Though God is merciful, He nevertheless punishes unto the third and fourth generation, as Moses says in **Exodus** <note>referring to Exodus 20:5 or 34:7</note>, because the malice of parents passes down even to the fourth generation. Children are therefore deprived of their paternal inheritance. This mirrors civil law, which dictates that the property of rebels and all who commit the crime of **high treason** <term>high treason: original Latin "crimen laesae maiestatis," literally "the crime of injured majesty," an offense against the sovereign or the state</term> shall be seized by the treasury <note>original: "fisco applicentur"</note>. Thus, the children remain deprived of their goods.

# DOGMAS

He foresaw all things from eternity without any change occurring in Himself; rather, mutability existed within the created thing, which received its existence externally, just as it had existed within the Word and Wisdom from eternity. Thus, the most wise Plato left it in writing that in God there is eternal providence and wisdom; in the heavens there is fate <note>original: "fatum"; in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the orderly laws governing the celestial spheres</note>; but in particular, earthly things there is the contingent and the new. Indeed, the final cause <term>causa finalis</term> <note>The ultimate purpose or "end goal" for which something is created</note>, which is the most significant, was this: that He might manifest His Wisdom—whom we have called the Son—externally. 

For this reason, the prophet sings: "In wisdom You have made all things" <note>original: "Omnia in sapientia fecisti"; a reference to Psalm 104:24</note>. This Wisdom and the Word <note>The Latin "Verbum" or Greek "Logos"</note> are the same thing, through which Word all things were made—specifically by God through His command or word alone. And because the Creator <term>Opifex</term> <note>Latin for "artisan" or "maker," a term often used by philosophers to describe God's role in fashioning the universe without physical tools</note> did not require any external instrument to produce creation, His Word alone was sufficient. 

This was also accomplished in a wondrous order; for since all things were brought into being by a certain ideal and intrinsic Word, what remained but to unfold through the spoken word that which had been conceived? And since all things were produced by the power of the Divine Name, by expressing those things contained within the power of that Name through a voice or command, they all came forth from that Name—just as branches, flowers, and leaves emerge from the trunk of a tree. Also by this Word, "the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth," as the Psalm sings <note>original: "Verbo Domini caeli firmati sunt..."; Psalm 33:6</note>. He **ascends** like a tender shoot out of the ground, and like a root from a thirsty land <note>original: "ascendit vt virgultum de terra, & sicut radix de terra sitienti"; a citation of Isaiah 53:2, a prophecy traditionally interpreted by Christians as referring to the humble origins of the Messiah</note>. -># DOGMAS #<-

According to this **power** <term>Power (virtus): In this context, it refers to a soul’s innate capacity or constitutional strength rather than moral virtue.</term>, the one who works receives a reward based on the condition of the coin, or the gift provided. Nor are species determined by abstract numbers or "voiced" units <note>original: "unitates vocales," likely referring to discrete, indivisible mathematical units used in counting.</note> which are not divisible—where the species of the number changes by the mere addition or subtraction of a single unit—but rather they are determined by a **natural number** <term>Natural number: In this philosophical context, a quantity that allows for continuous degrees or parts (like a physical string or a musical pitch) rather than just whole integers.</term>, whose units are divisible. This power is a certain force, determined by a specific degree, according to which a soul is capable of its own office, and receives it.

The **third presupposition** is that when the Sephiroth are named without qualification, it is understood to refer to all ten of them. 

The **fourth presupposition** is that <term>Gevurah</term> <note>The fifth Sephirah, representing Might, Severity, or Judgment.</note> is the **great North** <note>original: "aquilo magnus". For it is true that souls depend first upon the entire Trinity, yet especially upon the **Holy Spirit**, namely as to their essential being. After this, they enter *Gevurah* first, and then successively into the other Sephiroth. 

Therefore Moses says: "He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" <note>Genesis 2:7.</note>. For to breathe is the proper action of the Holy Spirit. And **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose views on the pre-existence of souls were often cited by Christian Kabbalists.</note> says that the Holy Spirit gives life to all. The origin of the soul, therefore, is immediately from the Holy Spirit. And since, after coming into being, they enter first into *Gevurah* as if into a **first bridal chamber** <note>original: "primum thalamum". A metaphorical description of the soul's first resting place or vessel within the divine structure.</note>, souls are therefore said to proceed from *Gevurah* with respect to the other lower Sephiroth of creation.

The **Work of Creation** <note>original: "opus de Bresith"; referring to *Ma'aseh Bereshit*, the study of the natural world and physics</note> is the wisdom of nature, and the **Work of the Chariot** <note>original: "opus de merchana"; referring to *Ma'aseh Merkavah*, the study of divine mysteries and metaphysics</note> is the wisdom of Divinity. And this twofold order is distinguished by the fact that the happy and blessed Cabalist finally transfers and translates all study, all effort, all counsel, labor, and diligence—and indeed the entire intention of his mind—from the sensible world to the intellectual world. 

The Talmudists <note>scholars focused on Jewish law and the literal/legal aspects of the text</note>, however, remain in the sensible world, and the soul does not transcend this universal world. Moreover, they assign the angels to daily ministries and to carrying out the impulses of the divine will, [seeking] the most high...

The number six, as the first **perfect number** <note>A number equal to the sum of its divisors (1+2+3=6). The next is 28</note>, is also uniquely suited to the **Supreme Architect God** <note>original: *summo Opifici Deo*</note> or to His creation itself. In God, nothing is lacking; likewise, when the number six is broken down into its members, nothing is left over, nothing is missing, nothing exceeds, nothing flows out or in, and it requires no outside help. Instead, it is equal and balanced; it relies and stands firm upon its own parts and powers. Among these three causes of heat, the third <note>The duration of exposure or "lingering."</note> is the most primary and the greatest for the reasons cited; for sometimes a man who is far from a fire is heated more than another near the fire, because <note>Original: ".f." for "scilicet," meaning "namely" or "to wit."</note> he has been heated for a longer time. 

The second cause, following that one, is the stronger direction of the rays <note>The angle at which the sunlight hits the earth.</note>: but the smallest cause of heat is the proximity of the heating body <note>The actual physical distance between the Sun and the Earth.</note>. 

Hence, in summer the sun is sometimes farther from us because it is in the **apogee of the eccentric** <term>apogee</term> <note>Original: "auge excentrici." The point in the sun's perceived orbit where it is farthest from the Earth.</note>, yet it heats our region more than in winter, when it is near the opposite of the apogee, because in summer the sun, approaching the **Zenith** of our heads, shines more directly upon us.

This river rises in Africa.

The **Tigris**, however, which flows toward the Assyrians, rises from a conspicuous spring on a plain in the region of Greater Armenia, where it flows more slowly. Here, as far as the borders of the Medes, it is called the **Diglirus** <note>original: "Diglirus"; a name for the upper Tigris also recorded by the Roman natural historian Pliny as "Diglito."</note>; afterward, it begins to be called the **Tigris**, because it seems to fly like an arrow: for the Medes call an arrow a *tigris*. <note>A popular ancient etymology; the Old Persian word for arrow is "tigra."</note> And it passes through *Zeroada* and *Tesbite*; the swifter **Arsanias** <note>A river in eastern Turkey, usually considered a tributary of the Euphrates.</note> flows into it. Later, it merges into the Euphrates.

The **Euphrates**, indeed, is said to rise in Mount **Patiedrus** <note>A mountain in the Armenian Taurus range.</note> of Greater Armenia; running through the same region, it separates Greater Armenia from Cappadocia, and flows into the Persian Gulf (which is called the **Red Sea** <note>In ancient geography, "Red Sea" (*Mare Rubrum*) was a broad term that often included the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean.</note>).

From this, we can reach no logical conclusion as to how these four rivers have the same origin, since they seem to rise from such distant places. Therefore, it remains to be said that the sea is the source of those four named rivers. But then there will be no particular place that might be called a garden, or a "paradise of delights," that is inaccessible to us. Whence that description of the rivers seems entirely *symbolic* <note>original: "typica"; meaning a "type" or figure that represents a deeper spiritual truth rather than a literal geographic fact.</note>, through which [they are un]derstood <meta>catchword: [un]derstood (telliguntur)</meta>

And because God possesses infallible knowledge concerning future contingents, it is because He knows things already done no differently than those yet to be done. Just as He knows what has already occurred infallibly and clearly, so He knows what is yet to occur infallibly. 

And although God possesses infallible and most certain knowledge of these future contingents, they will nevertheless happen contingently and not out of necessity. This is because the Divine will determined these things contingently—for He could have chosen not to determine them. Therefore, God’s knowledge does not impose necessity upon the things known by Him.

Hence, although God knows future contingents, He does not know them necessarily, but contingently; therefore, He is able *not* to know them <note>The author is arguing that because God is free, His knowledge is a result of His free choice to create a specific world, not a mechanical necessity</note>. For God knows future contingencies just as the Divine will decrees them. Truly, the Divine will determined them purely contingently and freely. 

Therefore, God knows future things contingently and freely. In a **composite sense** <term>composite sense|A logical distinction (sensu composito) used to analyze a statement where the conditions are taken together; here, it explores whether God's knowledge and the event's possibility of not happening can exist at the same moment</term> this is false—namely, that for the very instant in which He knew such a thing must be, for that same instant He could have not-known it. The difficulty lies in this: how the contingency of things and God’s infallible knowledge (or providence) can stand together.

Plato, in his book *The Republic*, says that in God there is infallible providence and [yet] the contingency of things. Aristotle, in the 11th and 12th books of the *Metaphysics*, places providence in God—citing the Chaldean fathers (that is, the Hebrews)—and in the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>Original Latin: *Perih.*, short for *Perihermenias*</note> and the second book of the *Ethics*, he establishes the contingency of things, saying: "we are the masters of our own acts" <note>Original Latin: *nos sumus nostrorum actuum Domini*</note>.

Augustine likewise says: "nothing is so much in the power of the will as the will itself" <note>Original Latin: *nihil est tam in potestate voluntatis, quam ipsa voluntas*</note>. And the Psalm [says]: "My soul (that is, my willing) is always in my hands" <note>Reference to Psalm 119:109; Original Latin: *anima mea... in manibus meis semper*</note>. 

But how these two are compatible with one another—namely, that an event is contingent, yet in God there is infallible providence, and in the heavens there is fate (as Plato feels)—is utterly difficult. And Ockham <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), an English Franciscan friar and scholastic philosopher known for "Ockham's Razor"</note> says that this has not yet been revealed to any mortal. # M V DOGMATA 63

...be said of itself. Therefore it is essential, and consequently necessary. Thus, every future event is necessarily future. 

To these objections, I respond and say that every **contingent future** is contingently future; because whatever has the power not to be future is not necessarily future, and that which is not necessarily future is contingently future. And I say that a <term>contingent future</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "contingent" event is one that is not determined by prior causes and could happen or not happen, often depending on free will.</note> is contingent both when it exists and when it does not; it has the potential to be. And even when it exists, it has the potential not to be. For example, when I am actually writing, my writing is a contingent thing; for I am able not to write, and every contingent future is of this kind. 

Regarding the first reasoning, it is said that if a contingent future event known by God is supposed not to happen, then it would also be established in reality that God never knew it to be future; consequently, if it does not happen, He is not deceived. For if the thing happens, God knows it contingently (for He could have not known it if the will <note>Referring to the human will's freedom to choose a specific path.</note> had not determined it to be future) and He always knows it as future; but if indeed it should never happen, He did not know it to be future.

Regarding the second, it is answered by denying the logical consequence. A "fallacy of speech" occurs there by arguing from a <term>composite sense</term> to a false <term>divided sense</term> <note>A classic tool of medieval logic. The "composite sense" looks at a statement as a whole: "It is impossible to sit and run at the same time." The "divided sense" separates them: "A man who is sitting is incapable of running." The fallacy lies in confusing the two.</note>. For this proposition is necessary in the composite sense: "one who sits is not running." From this, [the opponent argues] this will be true: "it is necessary for one who sits not to run." For...

Love is of such great power that no work of magic <term>magic: here meaning "natural magic," the philosophical art of understanding and utilizing the hidden sympathies and connections between all parts of the created world</term> can be performed without Love. According to **Plato**, the elements and all other things were united in the ancient **chaos** through friendship and love. 

Hence it pleased **Anaxagoras** <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who suggested that all things were originally a chaotic mixture until Mind (*Nous*) brought order to them.</note> to believe that through friendship and strife <term>strife: *lis* in Latin, referring to the force of separation or discord that breaks down structures</term> all things were generated and destroyed. However, once that universal friendship was relaxed—or rather, when strife arose among all things—these kinds of parts stood separated from the universal whole and were united with their own kind.

# OF THE CABALISTS #

[The first] is older, and born in heaven without a mother, whom we call the Celestial Venus <note>original: "cœlestem"</note>; the other, truly, is younger, born from Jupiter and Dione, whom we call the Vulgar <term>Vulgar: here meaning "common" or "universal," from the Latin *vulgaris*, rather than necessarily "crude"</term> and common. For that which is done with good and right love is honorable; and that which rests upon bad and distorted love is shameful and unbecoming.

Plato himself pursues this at length in that same work <note>This refers to Plato's *Symposium*, where the character Pausanias distinguishes between the two types of love</note>, which I leave to be read in its own place. Of these two Venuses, the Academics <term>Academics: the philosophical followers of Plato's Academy</term> call one "Ethereal" and the other "Aerial." The higher is pure, chaste, and orderly, in accord with Jupiter, connecting higher, divine, and spiritual things. The lower is disordered, slippery, changeable, and lustful, joining together animal life and things even lower than them. And regarding this lower Venus, so many obscene things are told by the poets, because she is the cause of all evils, just as the former is the cause of all goods.

Hence Augustine says: "Two loves made two cities: the orderly and good love of God, and the love of neighbors, reaching even to the contempt of oneself, made the City of God; but the inverted love of self, reaching even to the contempt of God, made the City of the Devil." <note>original: "Duo amores fecerunt duas ciuitates..." — This is a central theme from St. Augustine’s *The City of God*, distinguishing between those who live for the spirit and those who live for the flesh.</note> For this reason, the power of this star is called "Venus" by the grammarians because it "comes" <note>original: "veniat" — The author is using a traditional etymological argument, linking the name *Venus* to the Latin verb *venire*, meaning "to come."</note> to all things, namely to both the bad and the good.

...by its ray, it prevails over the worse and hostile fortune.

**According to the Cabalists** <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that explores the nature of the Divine</note>, however, there are two Venuses: **Tipheret** and **Malchut**, which are called the "two loves," even if they are one love through reciprocity. Whence **Solomon** in the *Canticles* <note>The Song of Songs in the Bible</note> introduces the bridegroom **Tipheret** <note>The sixth Sephirah, representing Beauty and the masculine divine principle</note> and the bride **Malchut** <note>The tenth Sephirah, representing the Kingdom, the Shekhinah, or the feminine divine principle</note> speaking to each other, especially in those words: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth* <note>original Latin: "Osculetur me osculo oris sui"; from Song of Songs 1:2</note>. 

These are the words of the bride **Malchut** addressing **Tipheret** himself, asking for that dimension, so that the gift of the **Holy Spirit**—or <term>Binah</term> <note>The third Sephirah, meaning "Understanding," often associated with the "supernal mother"</note>, which is called the "mouth of the Sephirot"—might flow into her. It is explained in another way, and first it must be noted that the numbers of the Hebrews are of two kinds: namely, the **greater** and the **lesser** <note>This refers to the systems of Gematria. The "greater" is the standard sum of letter values (*Mispar ha-Panim*), while the "lesser" is the reduced sum (*Mispar Katan*).</note>. The first arises from the particular values of all the individual letters of any word, so that it is the sum of them; just as in this name **Shaddai**, the greater number is **314** <note>Shin (300) + Dalet (4) + Yod (10) = 314.</note>.

The other is the **lesser number**, also called the **unequal number**: which takes a single unit from every hundred, and a single unit from every ten, while leaving any number less than ten as it is. In this way, **Shaddai** [שדי] signifies **8**; because the letter **Shin** [ש] yields 300, and thus in the lesser number gives 3 (by taking one for each hundred); **Dalet** [ד] gives 4 and remains a whole number; and **Yod** [י] signifies ten, from which a single unit is taken. And so the sum of these will be 8, and such is called the lesser number. 

Similarly, **Satan** and **Yod, He, Vav, He** <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter sacred name of God.</note> yield the same lesser number, in this way: **Satan** [שטן], **Shin** [ש] 300, **Tet** [ט] 9, **Nun** [ן] 50: all of which yield the lesser number **17** <note>Calculation: 3 (from 300) + 9 + 5 (from 50) = 17.</note>. **Iod-He-Vav-He** [יהוה], **Yod** [י] 10, **He** [ה] 5, **Vav** [ו] 6, **He** [ה] 5. All of these yield the lesser number **17**, as I said above <note>Calculation: 1 (from 10) + 5 + 6 + 5 = 17. # DOCTRINES

Concerning *chasak* [חֲשַׁךְ], it signifies that it grew dim, was obscured, or was darkened; from which comes *machshak* [מַחְשָׁךְ], that is, obscurity. In its construct form, *chaschim* [חֲשֵׁכִים] means those who are obscure or ignoble <note>This refers to those of low status or "in the dark" regarding spiritual truth</note>. Similarly, *Layelah* [לַיְלָה] signifies night, from which descends *Lilit* [לִילִית], which means the same: a wild animal, a lamia <term>lamia: a mythical female demon or monster often associated with the night</term>, a fury, or according to others, a bird that cries out at night <note>likely a screech owl</note>. Others think that it is an animal that wanders in the shadows of the night. The Masters <note>Referring to Rabbinic scholars or Kabbalists</note> also use this name for a "familiar demon," household spirits <note>original: *lares*</note>, ghosts <note>original: *laruas*</note>, a melancholy apparition, and other such specters. *Layish* [לַיִשׁ] also signifies a great lion of many years. Our translator <note>likely referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> renders this as "tiger."

Thus, they are very aptly described as: an animal walking in shadows, unable to enjoy the light of day. For this reason, he can be called a "Lion of many years," since from the start of his existence he began to be a nocturnal and obscure animal. ### OF THE KABBALISTS

[...it will possess] the quality of <term>choshech</term> <note>original: *chosech*; Hebrew: חֹשֶׁךְ</note>, that is, of darkness: specifically, how it stands in opposition to the light. It also possesses the quality of <term>laylah</term> <note>original: *laiela*; Hebrew: לַיְלָה</note>, which is night (this being the secret of darkness). For both of these terms signify a darkness that is set against the light. One will then understand why the evil ones, and so on, act as they do: because they refused to admit that light. Therefore, as <term>Job</term> says, they were rebels against the light <note>A reference to Job 24:13: "They are those who rebel against the light; they do not know its ways."</note> and were struck by darkness. Their leader in that rebellion was called and made the Prince of Darkness. To his service come all those who have been darkened—those who neglect to look up toward that light which "enlightens every man." For as <term>John</term> testifies, he who does evil hates the light <note>A reference to John 3:20</note>.

Yet, they are not entirely removed from that light; for they still receive the benefit of the light by which they live. We receive two primary benefits from light: one is the life by which we live, and the other is the light, or radiance, by which the light itself can be seen. Those who are in darkness, therefore, live but do not recognize it; for as the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato who argued that even the lowest forms of existence contain a trace of the divine source</note> say, the light remains even in the darkness. Just as cold relates to heat, and whiteness to blackness, so darkness relates to light. But just as there is a tiny amount of white in blackness, and a small amount of heat in cold, so too in the darkness there is a small measure of light—enough for them to live, but not enough for them to understand. And such are the <term>Demons</term>; for this reason, they are in accord with darkness.

From this we are taught that miracles are not to be sought where nature is able to assist: for to do so is to abuse divine power, and to yield to curiosity or vain glory, as is the case for one who desires miracles without necessity. And for this reason, Christ ordered those water-jars to be filled with water, because, as we have said, water is the matter most closely related to wine: for wine is nothing other than water distilled through the vine. Therefore, the form was introduced into the already-prepared matter without departing far from the natural progression. There are, however, other mysteries <note>original: *sacramenta*; here meaning hidden or sacred meanings</note> included here, which I leave aside for now.

Then, the priest would dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle the horn of the altar, while the rest was poured at its base. All those animal sacrifices correspond to that attribute.

From the **Cherubim**, we receive the light of the mind, or those super-exalted images and figures by which we are able to contemplate divine things. ### ->OF THE CABALISTS<-

...ate. This name is not found in the text of the Bible; it is, however, a symbol and seal of the ineffable **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: the holy four-letter name of God (YHVH), often considered too sacred to pronounce.</term>, and it proceeds from the final alphabet, which is the twenty-second of the *Book of Formation* <term>Sepher Yetzirah: one of the oldest and most influential books on Jewish mysticism, describing how the universe was created through the Hebrew letters.</term>. It is called **Athbash** <term>Athbash: a method of encoding text where the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, and so on.</term>. In that system, the letter *Yod* (י) is exchanged for *Mem* (מ), *He* (ה) for *Tzadi* (צ), and *Vav* (ו) for *Pe* (פ). Thus, it becomes **Mazpaz** (מצפץ) <note>original: "mazpaz." This is a "hidden" version of the name of God (יהוה).</note>, representing the Tetragrammaton when it is pronounced as **Adonai** <note>original: "Adonai," meaning "My Lord." Because the name YHVH is sacred, it is traditionally read aloud as Adonai.</note>. 

This name is attributed to the Kingdom of David, called **Malchut** <term>Malchut: the tenth Sephirah, representing the "Kingdom" or the physical realm where divine energy finally manifests.</term>. The reason is that this name is composed of *Maz* (מצ), which in Hebrew—within the sixth order of the conjugation of Hebrew verbs—and *Maza* in the fifth order, means "he sucked" or "he milked." It refers to an extractor, an emulsor, and a plunderer of the people <note>The author is using a metaphor here: just as a ruler "draws" from the people, this spiritual state draws divine energy from above.</note>. This fits **Malchut** appropriately, for **Malchut** draws out the "milk" of the influence of all the higher **Sephirot** <term>Sephirot: the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite God interacts with the universe.</term> toward itself. It acts as the womb <note>original: "matrix."</note> of all the higher **Sephirot** and is the "plunderer" of the nations, for it is that which renders to each person according to their works; it transfers the kingdom from nation to nation because of their injustice. 

It is also composed of *Paz* (פץ), which means to open or to free one who is bound. In the first conjugation, it is the same as lifting the voice, shouting for joy, rejoicing, and opening the mouth in song. In the second conjugation, it is the same as he shattered, he wounded, he cut apart, or a wound and plagues. All of these things agree with **Malchut**, for **Malchut** is the Gate of Entry to the Tetragrammaton.

->### OF THE CABALISTS ###<-

...its own fiery [nature], which after many rotations, having cast off the dross <note>original: *fecibus* — literally "dregs" or "sediment," representing spiritual impurity.</note>, returns all things that must be purged to the Creator <note>original: *opifici* — literally "the craftsman" or "maker," a term often used in Platonic and Hermetic texts to describe the Divine Architect.</note> now fully cleansed; so much so that they make their return to that same destined origin.

Circumcision was given for liberation from the unclean powers that walked in a circuit <note>In Kabbalistic thought, "those who walk in a circuit" often refers to demonic forces or "shells" (qliphoth) that surround the soul.</note>.

God, proceeding to the institution of sacrifices, commanded many things to be offered for various and diverse expiations. It should not seem harsh that God is delighted by the shed blood of animals, by roasted or burnt flesh, or by the fragrances of these and other things, as it is said in many places: *And the Lord smelled a sweet-smelling savor* <note>original: *odorem suauitatis* — a common biblical phrase (e.g., Genesis 8:21) indicating God’s acceptance of an offering.</note>. For this reason, these are held among the greatest **sacraments**.

Wherefore, to clarify this matter, it must be held that the most high God is delighted by no odors and no flavors; nor is He fed by the physical food of animals, nor by prepared loaves smeared with oil or drenched in fat—even though all these things were commanded to be done in the Law. Rather, this was done as a **sacrament** <term>sacramentum: Here used in the sense of a "sacred sign" or mystery—a physical ritual that represents a deeper spiritual reality.</term> of those things which were truly to be performed by Christ, and of those things which must consequently be carried out by us: namely, by mortifying our members <note>A reference to Colossians 3:5, "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth," meaning to suppress physical desires to achieve spiritual growth.</note> and offering them as an acceptable sacrifice. The ancient sacrifices bore the "figure" or shadow of these spiritual truths. Furthermore, these rites were commanded so that those powers <note>Spiritual entities or accusing angels.</note>—which continually accuse us at the tribunal of God for the crimes we have committed and for all the good we have omitted—might be appeased.

...efficacy <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought from the previous page regarding the limited power of old rituals.</note>. Under the Law, no one was justified except for sins contracted through ignorance, or by a momentary lapse of the mind, and similar things. For the Law to truly justify a person, it must first remove sin and free the person from the slavery of sin and its debt. Second, it must make that person dear, accepted, and worthy of eternal life. Only then is a person said to be truly justified, because they worthily merit eternal life. 

Therefore, because mankind was deprived of eternal life on account of original sin, and was bound to eternal physical punishment in hell on account of actual sin <term>actuale [peccatum]</term><gloss>A sin committed by an individual's own choice and action, distinguished from "original sin" which is inherited from Adam.</gloss>, he remained subject to God’s wrath and displeasure. Thus, it was first necessary for him to be absolved and purged of both types of sin; and second, to be restored to God’s grace and made pleasing to Him so as to attain eternal life. 

Circumcision, however, was not able by itself to absolve one from original sin and slavery, nor could it restore a person to God’s grace or make them meritorious and worthy of eternal life. For that small piece of skin which was cut away, and the meager amount of blood shed during circumcision, were of very little value <note>original: *vilissimus* — literally "cheapest" or "most worthless," used here to contrast the physical flesh with the infinite value of the soul.</note> compared to the soul. Therefore, it was not a sufficient price to redeem the whole person—especially the soul—and thus it could neither redeem the soul nor free it from its debt. Similarly, neither the animals sacrificed under the Law, nor the offerings, nor the other sacraments of the Old Law...

### OF THE KABBALISTS

</center>

**F. A.** The Law is of such great dignity that David, in admiration, says: *Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law* <note>Psalm 119:18. In this context, "the Law" refers to the Torah, viewed by Kabbalists as a mystical map of the divine mind.</note>. For in the Law are the wonders of the Gospel, with which the Law was pregnant. In the Law is taught the **construction of the World**, and its manner: from where the species of things come, their order, forms, matter, and operation, and what the ultimate end of all things may be. Through the Law we are instructed by what path and by what journey we may proceed toward God. In the same place, we are instructed concerning the past and future events of things, and that all things happen by the providence of God.

There we are taught concerning the concord and wondrous harmony of things among themselves and with God. Furthermore, without controversy, the **Ideas** <note>original: "Ideæ." Following the Platonic tradition, these are the eternal archetypes or blueprints of all created things existing within the divine mind.</note> are shown there: in which there is such power (as <term>Augustine</term> rightly judges <note>A reference to St. Augustine’s "On Diverse Questions," where he argues that no one can be wise without understanding the divine Ideas.</note>) that unless they are understood, no one can be wise. For there the most hidden **intelligences** <note>Spiritual or angelic beings that govern the celestial spheres.</note> are signified to each of us, as well as our commerce with them—indeed, even our fellowship with God—and how we can draw Him to us, so that we may be filled by Him, and He may act more familiarly with us.

And (what is even greater) in the Law we are taught how we can be **transformed into God himself** and become Gods <note>original: "Dij effici possimus." This refers to *theosis* or deification, the mystical process of being united with the divine nature.</note>. But these things are related in such a hidden mystery that those who are unworthy, "seeing may not see, and hearing may not understand" <note>A paraphrase of Isaiah 6:9 and Matthew 13:13.</note>. Therefore, the Law teaches us to ascend to God, so much so that the <term>Gospel</term> sends us to the Law, saying: *If you wish to enter into life, [keep the commandments]* <note>Matthew 19:17.</note>.

F. A. The law is of such great dignity that David says in admiration: *Open my eyes, and I will consider the wondrous things of your law.* <note>Psalm 119:18. In the law, the construction and the way of the world are taught: from where the species of things, their order, forms, matter, and operation come, and what the end of all things may be. Through the law we are instructed by what path and by what journey we are able to proceed toward God. In that same place we are instructed concerning the past and future outcomes of things, and that all things happen by the providence of God. 

There we are fully taught concerning the concord and wondrous harmony of things among themselves and with God. Also, without controversy, the Ideas <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "Ideæ." Here referring to the Platonic/Augustinian concept of eternal forms or archetypes in the mind of God.</note> are shown in that same place, in which there is such great power (as Augustine rightly feels) that unless these are understood, no one can be wise. And (what is greater) in the law we are taught how we may be transformed into God Himself and be made gods <note>original: "Dij effici possimus." This refers to the concept of *theosis* or divinization—the mystical process of becoming god-like through union with the Divine.</note>. 

But these things are related in such an occult mystery that those who are unworthy, though seeing, do not see, and though hearing, do not understand. Therefore, the law teaches us to ascend to God, just as the Gospel sends us to the law, saying: *If you wish to enter into life,* <note>Matthew 19:17. Regarding the letters, let these few things now suffice. Let us approach the *apices* <note>ornamental marks or strokes in writing</note>, which are twofold: namely, the lower and the upper. The lower ones are for the most part called "points"; in Hebrew they are called *negudoth* <term>Nekudot: the system of dots and dashes used as vowels in Hebrew, which is otherwise written only with consonants</term>, that is, those things which "give life" to the letters: for letters without points exist as dead, because they cannot be moved or pronounced.

The upper *apices*, however, which are called "accents" by us, are called *tagnamim* <term>Ta'amim: cantillation marks or accents used to indicate the musical chant and grammatical structure of the Hebrew Bible</term> in Hebrew, that is, they signify the Divine Holy Spirit: for by their mystery they lead us back to God. A dirty and infected eye, not yet well cleansed or weak, if it is directed toward a most brilliant spectacle, will immediately grow dim: for it is necessary that the one who is to see becomes kin and similar to the thing seen before they are applied to the viewing. For the eye would never see the sun unless it had become solar-like <note>original: *solaris*. This is a famous Neoplatonic concept from Plotinus: the eye must share the nature of light to perceive light.</note>, nor again would the soul [perceive beauty] unless it had become beautiful and Divine: then it will gaze upon beauty itself and God. After descending from Sinai, Moses' face radiated light so brightly he had to wear a veil.</note>.
