-># OF THE CABALISTS<-

[These] are the garments through which we are able to know God, whom we cannot grasp in His naked and pure essence. The "members" <note>Referring to the physical attributes like hands or eyes mentioned on the previous page.</note> are manifold powers within that one, most simple Being. And the "garments" are certain pathways through which He pours Himself out into us. While through these members—that is, through His manifold powers—He acts toward us, within Himself He performs a single, unified action. 

The Cabalists discuss these garments in the *Ilan* <note>original: "Ilan." Hebrew for "Tree," referring to the diagram of the divine structure.</note>, or the Tree of the *Sephirot* <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>. It is through these garments that every power emanating from Him proceeds; for from "naked" God, who is utterly removed from every relationship, nothing flows. This is because He contains all things within Himself as the fountain of all goodness. In the act of flowing out, He takes on a certain relationship, which they call a "garment." 

There are ten such garments. Indeed, God is said to be "naked" when He is considered in His naked and pure essence, utterly removed from any relationship—whether arising from within or from without—insofar as He is here, communicating Himself to no one. And He is called *Ensoph* <note>original: "Ensoph." From the Hebrew *Ein Sof*, meaning "The Infinite" or "Without End."</note>, about which [is written] in the conclusions of [Pico della] Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a Renaissance philosopher who sought to reconcile Kabbalah with Christian theology.</note>.

# D O G M A S

...[he] infers a thought from the previous statement, saying: "Love and fear lead to every sin." For just as the love and fear of God draw one toward every good, so the love and fear of the world drive one toward every evil. From this, <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> wishes to signify that there are two loves, and likewise two fears: namely, filial and servile. 

The first <note>Filial fear (from the Latin *filius*, meaning son).</note> is when someone fears God's commandments, not out of fear of punishment, but out of fear of paternal offense—that is, lest His honor be diminished and God be held in contempt—not considering whatever punishment might be due to him for such an offense. This is called intrinsic fear, and such a fear is more perfect than love, for it presupposes love. For he does not fear because God is powerful, but he fears because He is good. And this is what is usually said in the proverb: "The good fear to sin out of love for virtue" <note>original: "Timent peccare boni, virtutis amore." A classical maxim, often attributed to Horace, suggesting that the virtuous act rightly because they love goodness itself, not because they fear being caught.</note>. 

The other is the fear called servile, when someone has only punishment as their end, like a slave who fears to offend his master lest he be beaten. In this way, love is more perfect than fear. 

But, because the author's intention tends in another direction, note that through these double fears and loves mentioned above, two dimensions are understood—or <term>Sefirot</term> <note>original: "sephirot"; the ten attributes or emanations in Cabala through which the Infinite reveals Itself.</note>: <term>Ghedulah</term> <note>original: "ghedulah"; Hebrew for "Greatness," the attribute representing Divine Love and Mercy.</note> of love, and <term>Gheburah</term> <note>original: "gheburah"; Hebrew for "Strength" or "Severity," the attribute representing Divine Fear and Judgment.</note> of fear. It is also moved **accidentally** <term>per accidens: a philosophical term meaning something moves because the thing it is contained in moves (like a passenger in a boat), rather than moving by its own physical displacement.</term> according to the motion of the body. Yet it is a true motion, since it possesses the principle of motion within itself and is not moved by another.

And the **soul** has a **number** within itself—namely, a **rational number**—which is to say, it contains the **species** <term>species: here meaning the "forms" or mental blueprints of objects.</term> of things within itself, by which it understands them, and the numbers of things by which it counts them. And that is the **rational harmony** of which we speak, together with **Pythagoras** and the **Platonists**.

Nonetheless, the soul falls far short of the first and supreme **Intellect** <note>Referring to the Divine Mind or God, which perceives all of reality in a single, eternal instant.</note>, which understands all things simultaneously. Our soul does not understand everything in actuality and in a single act of intellection like the first Intellect; rather, it does so through many and successive acts. Therefore, the **intellectual soul** is a certain entity containing all things in a certain fitting arrangement, so that all things meant to be understood by it can indeed be understood.

Therefore, all the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" (covered walkways) of the Lyceum in Athens where Aristotle taught while walking.</term> said that all souls were produced in equal degrees, and continue to be so produced. Their foundation is the saying of **Aristotle**, who says: **"Species are like numbers,"** in which, if one unit is varied, the species is changed. For if a unit is added to the number three, the species changes and it becomes the number four. However, more recent theologians say that souls differ not only in **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential qualities—such as height, hair color, or learned skills—that can change without changing what a thing fundamentally is.</term> but in intrinsic degrees rooted in their very **essence**, by which each thing is *this* specific thing, differing from another through that which is its own property; for everything is distinguished first by its own nature, which is this, before...

...had made, and they were **exceedingly good**. <note>original: "fecerat, & erant valde bona." A reference to Genesis 1:31: "And God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good."</note> As a general rule, absolutely everything that God **made** is good, yet not everything that he **created** is so: for "to make" concerns the good, while "to create" concerns evil. However, since "to make" ends in "form," which possesses the nature of the good, He is therefore said to be "making good." Thus, whatever things decline toward matter have the nature of evil, and those which approach more closely to the highest form have, to that same degree, the nature of the good.

Therefore, that soul which is created more from the "coarser part" is called evil, while that which is truly from the "purer part" is called good. And such a good soul comes from the east. Souls that are already pure do not need to pass through this refining stage.</term>. This is because it contains no imperfection in itself to be purged by **Gheburah**. Those who are evil, however, make their journey through **Gheburah**, so that by its fire they may become pure from those dregs. And thus the conclusion is clear according to the Cabbalists.

# OF THE CABALISTS

<meta>catchword: from Aleph</meta>

F. A. Two Worlds are accepted by the Cabalists: the corporeal and the incorporeal, the visible and the invisible, the sensible and the mortal, the material and the ideal. These are the Lower World and the Upper World. They find this when they read: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* <note>Genesis 1:1</note> Thus, they believe that, symbolically, "heaven" designates the highest things and "earth" the lowest things. They interpret it in this way: "In the beginning, God created the highest and the lowest." By this, they mean that the simple and immaterial World contains the highest things, while this dense and physical <note>original: "commentarium," likely referring to the "commentary" or manifest world of matter</note> world contains the lowest. 

For this reason, the divine law promulgated as *Bereshit* <note>The Hebrew title of the Book of Genesis, meaning "In the beginning"</note> regarding creation began with the very letter **Beth** <term>ב</term> <note>The second letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>, which in the art of Arithmetic signifies the number **two**. It is as if it were noted to suggest that God principally created two things: the entire supreme World with everyone dwelling in it, and the entire lower World and all things pertaining to it. 

For if there had been only one world, it would have been enough for **Moses** to have written: *Reshit bara Elohim shamayim ve-aretz* <note>original: "Resit bara Elohim samaim vearez"; Hebrew for "A beginning created God the heavens and the earth"</note>. That is: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Indeed, that summary of creation could have avoided starting with the letter **Beth** <term>ב</term> (which signifies "In"), as the word for "beginning" can be placed without any preposition. 

Furthermore, contrary to usual custom, he added two "articles" to these two created things—that is, the word **Et** <term>את</term> <note>A Hebrew particle used to point to a definite direct object; Cabalists view it as a symbol of totality since it consists of the first (Aleph) and last (Tav) letters of the alphabet</note> appears twice. These are signs of all-encompassing inclusion, because **Et** <term>את</term> is composed of **Aleph** <term>א</term>...

# OF THE CABALISTS
<meta>catchword: every</meta>

Therefore, by those particles and **את** <note>original: "את"; the Hebrew direct object marker 'Et'.</note>, two conjoined propositions are understood: namely, an **ideal** heaven and earth, and a **physical and material** heaven and earth. Otherwise, there would have been no need for two connecting signs—"And" and **את**—if Moses had intended to speak of only one creation, that is, either the ideal only, or the physical only.

Through the first "And," therefore, the **ideal** production is signified; but through the second, the **real and material** production is understood as coming into physical existence. The **Cabalists** <term>Cabalistae</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the finite universe.</note> consider the first description in the manner mentioned before; but the **Talmudists** <term>Thalmudistae</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil law and biblical interpretation.</note> consider the second, saying:

> In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth:

By "heaven," they understand all things in the visible world that are above the Moon, and what is below it, they call "earth." Next, they also interpret "heaven" as **form** and they maintain that "earth" is **matter**. For this reason, they say that in the beginning:

> God created form and matter,

the composition of which He then forged into each individual thing by His divine decree. He did not shape everything with His hand so much as He hewed them nine times <note>This refers to the "Nine Sayings" of creation in Genesis chapter 1. While there are ten instances of "God said," commentators often distinguish the commands that brought matter into being.</note> with His word. For it is read:

> God said, "Let there be light." And God said, "Let there be a firmament." And God said, "Let the waters be gathered together." And God said, "Let the earth bring forth." And God said, "Let there be lights." And God said, "Let us make man." And God said, "Behold, I have given to you."

### DOGMAS. 213

...of heaven. And the same prophet repeats this title several times in chapter 44. For if you attend to these words of Jeremiah in the Hebrew copy, you will find that the word "Queen" is written one way in the main text, but read another way in the marginal note (which they call the <term>Masorah: the tradition of Jewish scholars who preserved the correct spelling and pronunciation of the Hebrew Bible</term>).

Specifically, it is written as *malcha* <note>original Hebrew: מלכת</note>, which means "Queen." In the margin, however, it is read as *Melachah* <note>original Hebrew: מלאכת</note>, which signifies "workmanship," "work," or "service." Whenever this kind of dissonance between the text and the margin is found in the sacred canon, it is certain—according to the Hebrew scholars—that some hidden mystery lies hidden there.

It is just like that great sacrament <note>The author uses "sacrament" here in the sense of a holy mystery or sign.</note> of the Passion indicated in the prophet Zechariah: "and they shall look," he says, "upon me whom they have pierced." <note>Zechariah 12:10</note> For there, in the main text of the copy, it is written as *Elai* <note>original Hebrew: אלי</note>, that is, "to me." In the margin, however, it is read as *Elau* <note>original Hebrew: אליו</note>, which means "to him."

By this, the Prophet wished to suggest that although God (who speaks through the mouth of the Prophet) announces Himself as the one pierced, it is not according to His nature as God, but insofar as He is man. Therefore, it is read in the margin as "to him," namely, to that same man as a man.

The same rule must be applied to the current judgment: for although they [the ancients] adore the celestial bodies and "workmanship," they do not do so insofar as they are mere bodies, but insofar as a soul and the gracious queen of heaven dwells within them. Nor [is the soul] of this...

...just as plants and animals are, but equivocally—namely, by such an equivocation <note>original: "aequivocatione," a logical term for when the same word is used to describe two very different categories of things</note> as when the term "body" is spoken of both celestial and earthly things. Second: The soul is the primary principle of life for the celestial body; therefore, the soul is the form or the actualizing force <term>actus: in scholastic philosophy, the "actuality" or the realization of a potentiality</term> of the celestial body. Third: Heaven is a more perfect body; therefore, its form is also more perfect—namely, the soul. Fourth: To be "animate" is a denominative description; such a description comes from a thing inherent in the subject by way of its form; therefore, the soul is inherent in the celestial body as its form. ### DOGMAS ###

is his footstool <note>original: "scabellum pedum eius"; a continuation of the quote from Isaiah 66:1: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool"</note>. But there is also that which the **Apostle** <note>Paul</note>, when he was preaching among the **Athenians**, said while approving the sentiment of **Aratus** <note>Aratus was a Greek poet; Paul quotes his *Phaenomena* in Acts 17:28</note>: **"Because in Him we live, and move, and have our being."** And how is this possible, unless it is because God, by His own power, binds together, contains, and vivifies <note>original: "viuificat"; to give life or soul to</note> the entire **World**? For this reason, it is said that the soul is everywhere. ->## DOCTRINES<-

...namely God, the common acting nature, who, being diffused throughout all things, grants to all the power to act. And thus, God is everywhere and nowhere.

For this reason, "place" can be considered in two ways according to the **Theologians** <note>The author is likely referencing Scholastic thinkers like Thomas Aquinas, who famously argued that God is in all things by power, presence, and essence</note>: in one way, insofar as it is a specific created thing; and in this sense, God is in all places just as He is in all things. In the other way, place can be considered as a **container** <note>original: "contentiuus"</note> of the thing located within it. And in this sense, God, according to His own nature, is nowhere, because He is contained by nothing; rather, He contains and preserves all things. 

However, according to His effects, He is everywhere, because He fills every place with His effects. According to this mode, it is proper to God alone to be everywhere; for nothing fills every place with its goodness and its effects except God. 

Yet He is "nowhere" in a **containing** <note>original: "contentiuè"</note> or **circumscribing** <note>original: "circunscriptiuè"; a technical term for how a physical body occupies space by having its boundaries defined by the surrounding space</note> sense, because these qualities belong only to physical bodies. Nor is He there **definitively** <note>original: "diffinitiuè"; a term used for spirits like angels, who are in a place because they are acting there and nowhere else, thus being "defined" by that location</note>, because this belongs to created spirits. 

The reason is that both these modes imply limitation: the first implies the limitation of physical quantity; the second argues for a limitation of essence and power. According to neither of these two modes can anything be in several places at once, and much less everywhere. Truly, to be in a place **replenishingly** <note>original: "repletiuè"; filling a space through divine power or presence rather than through physical mass</note> belongs to God—not according to His essence in a physical sense, but according to His effects (as I have said)—and thus
